https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.title: Tailoring Twitter takes down the Tates
https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.text:
Good day, darlingest Times reader — I feel the loucheness of summer allows a more lubricious greeting; let’s face it, none of us will feel “darlingest” come November — and welcome to the week where it became impossible to ignore what has become increasingly obvious: evolution is working faster than we thought.
The past few months have had two seemingly disparate stories. The first: increasing moves, by geologists, to announce officially that we are now in the Anthropocene Age. Plastic pollution, nuclear fallout and the climate crisis are now so widespread, they will have made it into the future geological record. We are at the beginning of a world formed primarily, not by nature, but by humans. To misquote the pirates in Captain Phillips, “We are the captain now.” There is nothing more powerful than us.
The second story — seemingly unconnected — has been the rise in animals who are, frankly, off their tits. Recent Celebrity Watch columns have chronicled the hit movie Cocaine Bear — based on the true story of a bear who ate a bag of cocaine. The following week we had the story of how marine biologists are convinced that large sealife — dolphins, orcas and sharks — are also ingesting not only cocaine but also methamphetamine, crack and ketamine. Drug cartels, it seems, keep dumping their wares, and the beasts keep munching them. Fair enough.
And now to this week’s third story, which appears to provide some manner of twist: a bear going nuts on a plane.
“Bear runs amok on a plane after breaking out of its cage in the cargo hold just before take-off in Dubai”, as the endless headline at MailOnline put it. Video footage confirmed the headline: if you’ve ever wanted to see an Iraqi Airways employee open what is, basically, the boot of a plane to see the huge, looming face of a bear roaming around the hold, that footage is available to you.
So, what’s the twist? Well, I don’t want to Columbo the situation overly, but animals getting off their tits on class As? Animals behaving like dicks on long-haul flights? It seems like animals have started . . . copying humans. They’re not picking up on this behaviour from anyone else. This is classic us. If this were at school, the head of pastoral care would treat this as an open-and-shut case of more impressionable kids (the animals) copying the naughty kids (us), presumably in order to fit in.
Which is why I suggest that what is happening here is that evolution is working far faster than we thought. The animal kingdom has noticed we’re in the Anthropocene Era, it knows humans are Top Dog. And it has observed that, somehow, we have become Top Dog even though we’re off our tits on class As and going berserk on long-haul flights — that, somehow, our carelessness and recklessness seem to be working for us.
So it has evolved. Animals are acting like dumb humans too.
Expect, in forthcoming weeks, a couple of moose joy-riding in a car; some crows playing the stock exchange; and 6,000 African grey parrots launching whimsical podcasts.
Do we expect Elon Musk to be consistent? I mean, I would guess “we” — me and you — couldn’t care either way. Peevish, rocket-building billionaires come and go, and they leave our lives, generally, untouched.
But as Musk is the on/off richest/most powerful man in the world, there are people — investors, markets, board members, lawyers — who would hope for some kind of . . . through-line? Given which, Musk’s latest pronouncement will have caused a big “hmm”. The subject? Freedom of speech on Musk’s latest, rapidly breaking toy: X, née Twitter.
“If you were unfairly treated by your employer due to posting or liking something on this platform, we will fund your legal bill,” Musk posted to his 152.3 million followers this week. He added there was “no limit” to the amount he would fund.
Musk’s thinking here seems to be that he dislikes censorship — and “wokedom” — and that he wants posters on X to say what they wish, without fear of being fired by “libtard” employers. How both principled and generous!
There is a problem, though — and it is, as is so often the case, with Musk himself. For, in 2022, a Twitter employee, Eric Frohnhoefer, tweeted a mild, technical disagreement with Musk — and Musk fired him. In a tweet. Which is, surely, “unfair treatment”.
So, now, theoretically, Frohnhoefer could ask Musk to fund his legal bill against Musk — for infringing his freedom of speech on X. Just how much does Musk believe in freedom of speech? Or, more crucially, ever think about what he’s saying?
“It’s the one thing Beyoncé demands on tour,” the headlines teased, promising to show us this special object if we clicked on the headline. “Every Beyoncé rider contains this item!”
Being a “click now, think later” kind of person, I clicked, and learnt that Beyoncé brings with her, on tour, an entire flight case filled with . . . lavatory seats. Her own, personal seats, which are fixed to every loo she might encounter between the dressing room and the stage.
Of course in one way this is quite extreme: for better or for worse most of us simply have to make do with whatever loo seats the day confronts us with, and the idea of having some manner of lav veto is simply unthinkable.
On the other hand, multiple outlets wrote this up as the behaviour of a “diva”. A diva? Really? Let’s have a quick run-down on what the most popular male pop stars have indulged in over the years. Heroin. Riding motorbikes into swimming pools. Biting the heads off bats. Fourteen-year-olds.
By way of comparison, having your own lavatory seat is, at worst, “fussy” and, more broadly, simply comes under the descriptor “hygienic”.
If anyone ever says there aren’t double standards when it comes to the way we judge women, just remember the mother-of-three Beyoncé trying to ensure she has a peaceful five minutes on the lav, before singing Single Ladies in front of 50,000 people, being called a “diva”, and draw your conclusions accordingly.
● The diva is back, and she’s been reinvented for the modern era
As many will know, this year’s World Scout Jamboree — held in South Korea — has been a bit of an . . . iffy woggle. A heatwave, followed by a typhoon warning, meant that conditions hit “character-forming” very early. As the camping fields first flooded, then became beset with mosquito swarms — and were then desperately strafed with industrial quantities of mosquito spray — social media flooded with pictures of sad-looking Scouts lying on the floor, captioned, “Are we going to die?”
As the South Korean government had, apparently, spent £60 million on the jamboree, the opposition parties have had a field day over the failed event — calling it “the real-life Squid Game”.
It has been, no two ways about it, a debacle.
And yet it’s also worth putting into some perspective. Scouts are aged between 10 and 14 years old — definitely too young to take part in Squid Game. And yet, by the time they’re 16, many of these Scouts will celebrate the end of their GCSEs by attending either Leeds or Reading Festival. Here they will be, once more, subject to rudimentary camping conditions in either heatwave or flood; will ingest huge clouds of chemicals — but, this time, in exchange for money; and will also probably spend a portion of their jamboree lying face-down on the floor asking, “Are we going to die?”
So, in a way, being a Scout will have made them “prepared”. It all kind of works out, in the end.● Thousands of British scouts pulled from South Korean jamboree
It’s so Canadian, isn’t it? When Italian prime ministers have a scandal, it’s over “bunga bunga” parties. When American presidents have a scandal, it’s over both fomenting insurrection and keeping classified documents in the “world’s most Hampstead Garden Suburb” en suite bathroom.
Canada? Canada’s a bit different. Canadian PMs announce that while they’ve had “meaningful and difficult conversations” with their wives, and will “remain a close family with love and respect for each other”, they are getting divorced.
Pierre Trudeau — then the prime minister of Canada — divorced Margaret Trudeau in 1984. Now his son Justin is continuing the tradition: by being both prime minister of Canada and announcing his divorce from his wife, Sophie Grégoire.
As if to continue the theme of Canadian reasonableness, Trudeau’s office noted that the family would continue to raise their kids in a “safe, loving and collaborative environment”, and that the whole family would be “together on vacation, beginning next week”.
It’s all admirably calm.
However. I couldn’t help but notice, buried in all the official announcements, the information that Sophie Grégoire has already moved out, into her own home — leaving the couple’s three children at the prime minister’s official residence, with their father.
In the majority of divorces, when primary custody is given it is awarded to the mother. What, I wonder, has been the deciding factor here? When my parents divorced, in a manner far less “Canadian”, my father declared he would “win” by offering “the best” siblings a video camera if they “screwed over your mum” and “stayed with me”. Which, to be fair, totally worked.
Trudeau, of course, is able to offer his children the official, governmental Airbus; two official residences; and the constant presence of security provided by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Which is no small matter if you’re getting some shit at school but can call on six guys on horses to wade in, should Lee Bacon be stealing your lunch money.
Either way, it’s interesting to note that, when it comes to custody, the only way most fathers can hope to be seen as equal to most mothers is if they are one of the leaders of the free world. I can’t work out who will feel most vindicated by this: Fathers 4 Justice or Mumsnet.
● Justin Trudeau is a newly single man
This week Andrew Tate — the only controversial Big Brother contestant to eschew a relaxed and lucrative run in pantomime as King Rat in favour of running an alleged sex dungeon in Romania — issued another flurry of social media posts, including one that decried the “billions” of “dollars” British schools are now spending on deradicalising his male teenage fans.
“They are doing Anti Tate campaigns in schools,” he tweeted, visibly excited at being this generation’s Nick O’Teen.
However, for those schools resentful at having to divert funds that could otherwise eg teach children to read and write, some good news: you are not being left alone in your task. For, this week, an expertly whimsical social media user adopted a different, and very effective, tack in deflating the Tate Myth.
Andrew Tate’s younger brother, Tristan, is also accused of human trafficking, and is an equally avid social media user. To this end, this week Tate Jr posted a picture of himself in a suit, standing in front of an electric blue sports car so high-tech it looked, frankly, silly.
“I will wear perfectly tailored 20,000 dollar suits with diamond cuff links and hand made 14,000 dollar alligator shoes and I’ll STILL have holes in my socks,” he tweeted, adding, for context: “I’m from the streets. Never forget.”
“The streets” is a rum claim from someone whose father was a chess grandmaster and who was brought up in Luton, but, still, I guess Luton has streets. So it’s technically true.
Anyway. There it was. Would British schools now need to spend more “billions” counteracting this advert — with over one million views — for the Tate brothers’ Aspirational Way of Life? No. Because Tailoring Twitter rocked up and did the job instead.
“Tristan claims this suit costs $20k. That seems high to me, as a Savile Row suit typically costs ~$5k . . . Despite costing $20k, [this suit] doesn’t fit very well,” the menswear correspondent Derek Guy tweeted, with an audible “tut” in his voice, before letting loose the dogs of sartorial war. “[The] first thing is the divot in the sleevehead . . . [which] is often a sign the coat is too narrow through the shoulders and upper back . . . The lapels buckle away from the chest . . . creating drag lines around the waist,” he sighed. And “the trousers are also very narrow . . . The narrowness is causing the trouser leg to catch on the wearer’s calves, causing ripples below the knee.”
Guy continued this mannerly decimation of Tate’s tailoring snafu over ten subsequent posts — really stepping up a gear when he did a compare-and-contrast between the superlative tailoring in King Felipe of Spain’s trousers and the overpriced cowboy job done on Tate’s cruddy trews. By the end no one could be in any doubt: Tate Jr had dropped $20,000 on a suit that made him look like the young Norman Wisdom, but in a bad way, plus been stung for an unnecessary $15,000 he could have spent on badly needed socks. Or actually buying the car behind him, rather than — as I suspect — standing in front of someone else’s car then taking a selfie.
Personally I love this new Tate-levelling initiative. The idea of all non-Tate-like men taking it in turns to point out whimsically all the ways that Tateness is naff, ludicrous or idiotic is deeply healing. It feels like all the reasonable male elders of the tribe have finally realised that the younglings have been spending a bit too much time with Scar and are rocking up with some timely eye-rolling, then a bit of Hakuna Matata. Viva la Gentlemen’s Backlash!

https://www.thetimes.com/article/paris-2.title: Paris 2024: Britain’s track bike inspired by fighter-jet technology
https://www.thetimes.com/article/paris-2.subtitle: The Hope-Lotus is designed to win medals, not beauty contests, starting at the UCI World Championships
https://www.thetimes.com/article/paris-2.text:
The Hope-Lotus track bike that Great Britain will use at the UCI World Championships in Glasgow from Thursday — and the Paris Olympics next year — will win no prizes for beauty.
The forks and seat stays, the tubes which run from wheel to seat post are almost comically wide and the seat post itself has a hole in its centre. Elegance, though, does not distinguish a track bike — medals do. And this bike retains much of the unusual geometry of the 2019 model, with which Britain won seven medals at the Tokyo Olympics two years ago, the most of any nation.
Far from the unpredictability of the road, or any significant commercial pressures — the 2019 model cost more than £30,000 all told — the only real consideration for the Hope-Lotus is its contribution to a riders’ coefficient of drag area (CDA), which is to track-racing what weight is to a climber; that is, along with rider power, the main determinant of performance. This is how Great Britain’s new machine aims to optimise it.
From helmets to skinsuits or wheels, aerodynamic kit is designed to encourage the smooth flow of air around the rider, either by reducing skin friction or by reducing pressure drag. The most effective equipment encourages air to stick to riders and discourages the formation of “flow separation”, which is a low-pressure wake that effectively pulls a rider backwards.
The wide forks and seat stays follow this principle. Designed by Lotus, and constructed from the same carbon-fibre as its Evija “hypercar”, they are moved wider to be more aligned with the legs, encouraging the air to “stick” to the rider. By the same logic, during the hour records set by Dan Bigham and Filippo Ganna, the Q factor (effectively the distance between the pedals) was reduced, shifting legs in line with forks, though that position would probably be uncomfortable for most riders and significantly reduce their power output.
The ridges that run down the rider-side edge of the forks are the key difference with the 2019 model. A similar effect is used on some high-end carbon wheels, and were present on the seat post of the €70,000 Pinarello bike used by Ganna to break the hour record last year. Designed to encourage smooth air flow, Pinarello claimed that it was inspired by humpback whales. Lotus say their technology is derived from fighter jets. Either way, the influence of Bigham, a performance engineer at Ineos Grenadiers and a member of the GB team pursuit quartet, is probably not far away.
These developments are especially critical for track cycling, where speeds are highest (Ganna averaged more than 60km/h in setting the individual pursuit record at the World Championships last year), because the force required to overcome drag increases cubic velocity (if you double your speed, drag increases eight times).
There are two obvious flaws to calling this a seat post: it’s kinked and it’s got a hole in the middle. This is a significant change from the 2019 version, which was a more familiar fin-shaped carbon-fibre post. Instead, for the next two years at least, Great Britain will use this 3D-printed titanium contraption. As with the forks, this is designed to encourage smooth airflow. This sort of separation is not unprecedented; the American manufacturer Trek has a similar design on its flagship road bike, the Madone.
Although the frame is consistent from event to event, the handlebars change. For mass-start events such as the Madison, the omnium and the sprint events, the British team will run a reimagined version of drop handlebars. Rather than running flat and falling away, as is customary, they rise up first like a set of horns. For the pursuit events, there is a moderately familiar-looking set of aero handlebars.
Much of aerodynamic efficiency centres on rider position; both the position they can adopt and how long they can hold it. To ensure each athlete can sit in their preferred position, fine-tuned in a wind tunnel, Lotus say both aero and drop bars are fully customisable.
British Cycling experimented with the pitch of its chain — the distance between links — on the first edition of the Hope-Lotus, moving from the standard 1/2 inch to a 3/8 inch to allow more teeth on the chain ring without increasing its size, in theory improving drive-train efficiency. The chain alone, a Velo CT-T, cost £450.
To settle on the right tyre pressure on the road, a balance needs to be struck between minimising hysteric loss (energy given up when a soft tyre deforms) and damping losses (vibrations from rough surfaces). This usually sits at about 90 PSI, though it will be lower for a cobbled race where damping losses are greater. In a velodrome, however, where damping losses are negligible, the tyre pressure can be raised significantly, to between 180 and 220 PSI.
The correct disc wheels — which, again, encourage a smooth flow of air over the surface of the bike and rider — can lead to a significant energy saving, between 20 and 40 watts (or, depending on the rider, 5 to 10 per cent of the total power required). British Cycling is using a Hope wheel. The 2019 edition was available for £2,450 (rear) and £2,100 (front).

image.caption: The Hope-Lotus bike will get its first competitive outing at the UCI World Championships in GlasgowALEX WHITEHEAD/SWPIX.COM

https://www.thetimes.com/article/rishi-s.title: Rishi Sunak and family dress down for California holiday
https://www.thetimes.com/article/rishi-s.text:
Smiling in the California sunshine, Rishi Sunak and his family were a world away from the dreary weather at home as they posed for pictures while on holiday.
The prime minister opted for comfy plimsolls, a casual long-sleeve jumper and a simple pair of navy shorts as he posed with his wife, Akshata Murty, 43, and their daughters, Anoushka and Krishna, on Santa Monica Pier.
Once mocked for wearing £490 Prada driving shoes during a visit to a building site, Sunak, 43, slipped into £40 plimsolls from the high street brand Toms.
The prime minister’s wife wore a patterned £49.99 skirt from Zara. She also opted for a basic magenta scoop neck and Whistles woven bag — another buy below the £50 mark.
Their daughters looked to be enjoying their trip, both in suitably summery outfits for the day.
The prime minister’s high street choices were a far cry from his usual suits. He has previously been spotted wearing a two-piece suit by Henry Herbert that is thought to have cost £3,500.
Last month Tatler named Murty as one of the best-dressed people this year.
She wore £570 slippers from JW Anderson for the school run, and has been pictured in Gucci trainers that cost £445 and a leather skirt with a price tag of more than £1,000.
California holds a soft spot in the couple’s hearts as it is where they met and the place they once called home.
The family strolled along the pier, stopping to enjoy the stalls before their visit to Disneyland, where Sunak has said he will be dragging the girls to the Star Wars attractions.

image.caption: Rishi Sunak, his wife and their daughters started their holiday at Santa Monica PierEMMA MCINTYRE/GETTY IMAGES

https://www.thetimes.com/sport/football/.title: Andrew Tate v Amanda Holden: the King of Misogynists won’t win this one
https://www.thetimes.com/sport/football/.text:
Good day, dearest Times reader, and welcome to “drowned worms on the pavement” season, aka the British summer.
Of course in mainland Europe this is known, by way of contrast, as “frying worms on the pavement” season — the wide-raging dissimilitude in weather conditions reminding us that, whatever is happening with climate change, it’s always been pretty shit to be a worm.
However, as there is no “worm angle” on this week’s first story — I know, I’ve spent a long time trying to find it — we must now simply forget about the sorrows of global wormage and instead turn our attentions to the newest nightlife attraction in the northwest: Co-op Live in east Manchester.
With its first gigs now scheduled for June next year, the arena will be the biggest indoor music venue in the UK, with a capacity of 23,500, and boasts as one of its investors the World’s Sexiest Man, Harry Styles.● Move over London — there’s never been a better time for culture in the north
There is, however, just one small problem with this otherwise exciting and commendable endeavour. And it is easily observable to anyone who looks at a picture of Co-op Live: it looks undeniably less like Britain’s biggest indoor arena and more like the biggest ever branch of the Co-op. For at least its first six months of gigs, half the audience queuing up outside are going be confused — and possibly stoned — local students, hoping to get a packet of crumpets, a tub of Dairylea Cheese Spread and a packet of slim filters. There are going to be pensioners popping out for a bit of parmesan and ending up in the mosh pit for Wet Leg, and dads crowdsurfing to Sampa the Great, shouting, “This is the weirdest self-checkout ever! I love it!”
We all know that in social circles there’s always The First Person to Get into Drugs — the guy, and it usually is a guy, who then goes on to be the Drug Offerer to everyone else. In my teenage social circle that guy was a man nicknamed “Harry the Hoover” for both his ferocious ability to suck up anything and everything and the fact he often had to be unplugged, carried downstairs and then shut in a cupboard at the end of a long, long day.
Well, it seems that it’s not just humans who are easily influenced by a narcotic outrider! As cinephiles will know, one of the most talked-about movies of the past few years was Cocaine Bear, a ridiculous, camp romp inspired by the true-life story of an American brown bear that ingested a package of cocaine abandoned in the woods by a drug cartel. Inspired by Cocaine Bear’s box office, later this year we will be treated to Crackcoon — which is, yes, about a racoon that’s munched up some cartel-mishandled crack.
● Cocaine Bear: true story of unfortunate animal that inspired Hollywood film
And now, as part of some “animals on drugs” trilogy, this week the Discovery Channel broadcasts Cocaine Sharks, a documentary that speculates that recent “erratic” behaviour by sharks has been caused by them ingesting not only cocaine but also methamphetamines, ketamine and hallucinogens dumped off the coast of Florida by, once again, slipshod drug cartels.
“[Marine biologists] observed sharks exhibiting peculiar behaviours,” a report in The Guardian explained. “A hammerhead, a species that would usually swim away from humans, came directly towards the divers, moving erratically. They also observed a sandbar shark swimming in circles as it apparently focused on an imaginary object.”
Well, there’s a lot to unpack here. First of all: drug cartels! Are you using Evri to deliver your drugs? Because this whole “dumping packages in random places” technique seems awfully similar. And second: “aquatic creatures banging out mad rails of gak” does seem to explain the recent attacks from sharks, orcas and dolphins on human beings. It seems like much of ocean-going life has reached that point in the evening where it’s in full-on coke rage and swinging at strangers while eg some squid keeps shouting, “He’s not worth it, Free Willy! Flipper — let the human go!”
As we know, when America sneezes, the rest of the world gets out the antibac, so it’s worth noting that the latest hoo-ha to blow up “over there” is a song called Try That in a Small Town, which appears to be continuing the “culture war” trope of “country folk versus city dwellers”.
Try That in a Small Town, sung by Jason Aldean, has so far had more than 11 million streams and 24 million views on YouTube, and is ostensibly about how people in small towns are no-nonsense and take care of their own. “Cuss out a cop, spit in his face/ Stomp on the flag and light it up . . . Well, try that in a small town/ See how far ya make it down the road,” go the lyrics to this country-rock power ballad that is, in the parlance of the young people, “moist”.
However, as many have pointed out, the video for the song was shot on the steps of the Maury County Courthouse in Columbia, Tennessee, the site of both the 1946 Columbia race riot and the 1927 mob lynching of Henry Choate, an 18-year-old black teenager. The vibe is very much “if you come over here with your Black Lives Matter protests and ‘urban’ carjacking, there’s some ‘good old boys’ that will ‘take care’ of you”. The fact that the song has now been endorsed by Donald Trump — your worst nightmare host of Top of the Pops — has, of course, increased the fuss.
While it’s always instructive to keep a weather eye on America’s cultural palavers, the chances of Try That in a Small Town’s race war baiting being a hit in the UK seem relatively slim. All the inferences are just . . . different. Here, if someone says “try that in a small town”, they’re more likely to be challenging you ruefully to buy an onion after 5.30pm or download a .wav file in less than two hours.
● Justin Webb: Music is the latest front in the US culture wars
It is, as we know, tough being a new mother. The sleeplessness. The anxiety. The gigantically traumatic incident that happened in your pants area, which everyone just shrugs off as “natural”. The terrorists.
The terrorists? Yes — the terrorists. For this week an NHS midwife was struck off after telling a new mother that she should try harder to breastfeed her baby as terrorists could poison her formula milk.
Anna Semenenko, 59, faced multiple allegations of inappropriate behaviour at Royal Gwent and Nevill Hall NHS hospitals in south Wales. She took pictures of one patient’s “pretty” vagina; joked about another patient’s husband’s penis size (“it must be very small!”); and claimed she would get “ten male doctors” to give a third patient stitches. Like a patriarchy pain party! Fun!
But it was the claim that breastfeeding was important because terrorists might poison formula milk that had the “bossy” midwife struck off for giving “false and misleading” information. And they were right — it is misleading information, as terrorists would never be helpful enough to come to your house, make up a bottle and then pop some poison in it.
Which is a shame, because however much terrorists are being paid, the average babysitting fee an exhausted mother could offer them just to do the 2am feed would dwarf anything offered by Smersh.
The latest trend in the world of football is for a celebrity to bankroll a club — something that was kick-started by Elton John and Watford, continued with Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney’s purchase of Wrexham, and is now reaching its peak with fevered rumours of Tottenham Hotspur possibly being subject to a bid from the billionaire rap mogul Jay-Z.
Having googled “Tottenham FC”, I can see why Mr Beyoncé might be interested in purchasing said sporting institution. First, Jay-Z is, apparently, a Gooner, so might possibly be planning to aid his beloved Arsenal by bringing down Spurs “from within”. I gather these are the kinds of things football fans speculate about.
Additionally, Jay-Z infamously has a large car collection — as in, he has very large cars. If you own a $1 million, 1-tonne, 20ft x 8ft Dartz Prombron — an AK47-proof SUV with, and this is true, whale foreskin interior trim — it’s going to be a faff to buy Millwall, given all the associated parking nightmares of the Den.
Tottenham, on the other hand, is right next to a big Sainsbury’s, so Hova can pop the Prombron in an extra-wide space — or even in a “mother and child” space if he’s brought Blue Ivy and feels cheeky! — and then pick up a Charlie Bigham’s fish pie for Beyoncé on the way home.
And finally? The club moved to the new Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in 2019, which has state-of-the-art retractable technology that provides both turf and, beneath it, a synthetic NFL American football field.So Jay-Z might have 99 problems — but the pitch ain’t one.
Thank you. Thank you for listening to my joke.
And so it came to pass that, in the last week of July 2023, hard-right radicalised misogyny finally “went there” and attempted to provoke the online equivalent of JRR Tolkien’s Battle of Helm’s Deep.
In this instance, the pivotal Hornburg fortress is represented by the fragrant light entertainment figure Amanda Holden, while the battering ram manoeuvred against the fortress gate by Saruman’s Orc army is a bitchy tweet from Andrew Tate about . . . Holden’s bikini. Yes, this is ultimately what the culture wars are about: a black two-piece from, by the looks of it, Boden. And who is allowed to wear it, then post a picture of it on Instagram.
Holden presumably thought she could wear a bikini, then post a picture of it on Instagram — as she did last weekend. Obviously there are no laws, or even guidelines, against a 52-year-old mother of two posting a shot of herself on holiday taking a post-swim shower and looking, by all accounts, both hot and chill.
● Andrew Tate charged with rape and human trafficking in Romania● Schools tackle misogyny to counter toxic rise of Andrew Tate
Tate, however — both King of the New Misogynists and, perhaps not incidentally, facing charges of rape and sex-trafficking multiple women to Romania — saw things differently.
“You are a wife and a mother and youre far past a teenager. There is no need for this post,” he tweeted. Of course it’s easy to see why Tate tweeted: first, he’s just done six months under house arrest, waiting for Romania’s anti-organised crime agency to begin the prosecution of his alleged crimes. So he’s very, very bored. As a man in the sex-cam business, his internet algorithms would naturally serve him up a lot of “sexy lady” content — hence the picture of Holden coming up on his phone. Algorithms don’t lie! Algorithms know Andrew Tate is interested in sexy lady bums, such as that on eg Amanda Holden!
And this is quite the betrayal by Tate’s social media feed, for one of Tate’s more piquant beliefs is that women are at their best between 18 and 19, because by 25 — and I apologise for the language here — “they’ve had too much dick”.
As Holden infamously recurs on all “hottest women” charts — having won the Arse Nobel of “Rear of the Year” at 48, 30 years older than Tate’s “optimal” age — her bum makes an exquisitely poor choice of terrain for Tate’s Final Culture War Push. For if Tate’s latest wheeze is to sell to his audience of insecure, teenage boys a philosophy wherein Holden is believed to be a rancid old hag who needs to pop a poncho on and get off the internet, I believe he may finally have bitten off more than he can chew. You can’t go all Handmaid’s Tale on classic ITV1 light entertainment show totty. If Tate’s telling a bunch of pubescent virgins that Holden being a mother means she’s not hot any more, then he’s going up against one of the central premises of The Inbetweeners — that Will has a “fit mum”. And, when push comes to shove, teenage boys relate far more to the phrase “Bus wankers!” than Tate’s catchphrase of “Top G!”
